title: The Commission Ceiling: Why a Fully Booked Salon Can Still Be a Low-Margin Business
linkedin:
A salon's diary is fully booked through spring racing season and straight into the Christmas party run. Every chair taken, every treatment room full. It looks like the best few months of the year.

Here is the pattern we see once we look underneath that full column. Most salons and day spas pay stylists and therapists on a sliding commission scale, where the percentage rises once someone's personal takings pass a threshold. It is a sound retention tool.

It has a quieter side effect. Once a senior stylist steps up a commission tier, every extra dollar they bill in a busy season costs the business more than the same dollar from a team member still on the base tier.

So the busiest chair in the salon, run by the most booked out person on the team, is often the one carrying the thinnest margin per dollar of revenue, not the thickest. A season like this one pushes several senior team members past their threshold at once, and that effect compounds across the whole roster.

The fix isn't cutting commission. It's modelling what each tier actually costs before the season peaks, and making sure retail product sales, the one line a chair doesn't cap, are getting the same attention as the booking diary.

If you run a hair or beauty salon, day spa or similar appointment-based business on the east coast, this is worth a look before the spring racing and Christmas party season hits full swing. A fully booked appointment diary feels like the best possible sign, and in one sense it is, but it doesn't automatically mean the strongest margin.

Most salons pay stylists and therapists on a sliding commission scale, where the percentage paid rises once someone's personal takings pass a certain point. It's a sensible way to keep good people. The part that often goes unmodelled is that once a senior team member steps up a tier, every extra dollar they bill costs the business more than the same dollar from someone earlier in their career. In the busiest few weeks of the year, when several senior stylists or therapists cross that threshold together, the effect can show up across the whole roster at once, and the busiest chair in the salon ends up carrying one of the thinnest margins.

Retail product sales are one of the few places margin can still move without adding another hour to an already full day, and they are worth a closer look while foot traffic is guaranteed.
